title: Active-Passive
subtitle: Primary-standby topologies, fencing tokens against split-brain, and coordinated failover orchestration.
keyTakeaways: Active-Passive funnels all writes through a single Primary node/region while replicating state to one or more Standby nodes, preserving strict ACID serializability without multi-master write conflicts.

Split-brain, where an isolated old primary continues accepting writes after a standby is promoted, is the most dangerous failure mode and must be prevented using Quorum Leases and Monotonic Fencing Tokens.
Passive standbys suffer from 'cold cache' and 'untested path' risks; regular automated failover game-days and read-traffic shadowing are mandatory to prove RTO targets.

sections.heading: Primary-Standby Replication & The Split-Brain Hazard
sections.body: In an Active-Passive architecture, a single authoritative Primary orders all state mutations and streams a Write-Ahead Log (WAL) or binlog to Passive Standby instances. While passive nodes may serve read-only queries, all writes are serialized through the primary.
bullets: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Standby: Synchronous standbys guarantee zero data loss (RPO = 0) at the cost of write latency; asynchronous standbys (common across WAN regions) decouple primary latency but risk losing in-flight transactions on crash.

Anatomy of Split-Brain: If a network partition isolates the Primary from the health checker (or the Primary pauses for a 15-second JVM GC), the orchestrator promotes the Standby. If the old Primary wakes up and still processes client writes, two nodes corrupt state simultaneously.

STONITH & Fencing Tokens: True safety requires monotonically increasing epoch numbers (`fencing_token`) issued by a Raft/Paxos coordinator. Storage engines and downstream consumers reject any write carrying an epoch lower than the highest seen epoch.

sections.heading: Failover Detection Tuning, DNS TTLs, and Cold-Start Traps
sections.body: The total failover time (RTO) in Active-Passive is the sum of Failure Detection Time + Standby Catch-up/Promotion Time + Client Traffic Re-routing Time.
bullets: Flapping vs Fast Failover: Setting health-check timeouts too aggressively (e.g., 1 second) causes false-positive failovers ('flapping') during minor network jitter, whereas conservative timeouts (60 seconds) lengthen downtime.

DNS Caching Pitfalls: Relying on DNS record updates for failover is unreliable because corporate resolvers and JVM HTTP clients often ignore 60s TTLs. Prefer Anycast VIPs, proxy routing (PgBouncer/ProxySQL), or smart client SDKs that probe cluster topology.
Cold Buffer Pool Degradation: A passive database standby whose RAM buffer pool is not warm with the working set will suffer 10x disk I/O latency spikes the moment production traffic switches over.

tradeOffs.pros: Failover completes in seconds to a few minutes; standby immediately sustains 100% peak load.
tradeOffs.cons: Doubles compute and memory licensing costs for hardware sitting mostly idle (or serving only reads).
tradeOffs.bestFor: Relational databases (Postgres/MySQL), financial ledgers, and Tier-1 stateful services.

tradeOffs.option: Warm / Cold Standby (Scaled Down Until Failover)
tradeOffs.pros: Saves 60-80% on secondary compute infrastructure costs during normal operations.
tradeOffs.cons: RTO extends to 15-60+ minutes while cloud auto-scaling provisions nodes and warms caches.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Tier-2/Tier-3 enterprise apps, internal workflows, and non-realtime reporting systems.

interviewTip: Never say 'we just use a heartbeat to detect primary failure and promote the replica' without mentioning **Fencing Tokens** or **Quorum Leases** to prevent split-brain when the old primary only suffered an asymmetric network partition.
